lesson: TWO fixes only (review round 1). FIX 2 (performance P2): human-decision-memory-service.ts list() calls deriveHumanDecisionShortId(row.id, ids) per row, and that function re-normalises every sibling for every row and every prefix length — quadratic. Add an exported deriveHumanDecisionShortIds(ids: string[]): Map<string, string> that normalises each id ONCE, then resolves prefixes by counting: starting at length 6, build a Map<prefix, count> over the still-unresolved ids, mark ids whose prefix count is 1 as resolved at that length, and extend the rest by one character until resolved (O(n × average prefix length)); list() computes the map once and reads shortId from it; keep deriveHumanDecisionShortId(id, siblings) with its exact current semantics as a thin wrapper over the batch function (the contract and the unit leaf name it). Add one unit case: 500 ids with a shared 6-char prefix on two of them resolve in one call with only those two extended to 7. FIX 1 (quality P2): putHumanDecision does select-then-insert inside its transaction with no lock, so two concurrent FIRST writes for the same (app_id, agent_folder, acting_person_id, scope, scope_key) race the partial unique index and the loser throws instead of refreshing. Fix at the top of the transaction, before the select: await tx.execute(sql) — a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on the human authority, released at commit; the same pattern as canonical-message-attachment-lock.postgres.ts and live-admission-work-item-repository.postgres.ts — then keep the existing select/refresh/insert unchanged. Prove it in the Postgres suite with one new case inside the existing round-trips leaf (do NOT add a new it() and do NOT change any title): Promise.all of two putHumanDecision calls for the same key with different ids resolves to one inserted and one refreshed sharing the stored id, and exactly one active row exists.
